questions.q: What is ethics?
options: A set of moral standards for judging whether something is right or wrong
questions.explain: Business ethics starts with recognising an ethical issue.
questions.evidence: Ethics is a set of moral standards for judging whether something is right or wrong.

questions.q: What is an ethical issue?
options: A situation where someone must choose between actions that may be ethical or unethical
questions.explain: Recognising ethical issues is the first step.
questions.evidence: An ethical issue is a situation where someone must choose between a set of actions that may be ethical or unethical.

questions.q: What is the first step in understanding business ethics?
options: Learning to recognise an ethical issue
questions.explain: You can only respond to issues you recognise.
questions.evidence: The first step in understanding business ethics is learning to recognize an ethical issue.

questions.q: What does a code of ethics give employees?
options: Knowledge of what the firm expects in their behaviour toward colleagues, customers and suppliers
questions.explain: Most large companies have written codes of ethics.
questions.evidence: In general, a code of ethics provides employees with the knowledge of what their firm expects in terms of their responsibilities and behavior toward fellow employees, customers, and suppliers.

questions.q: Why does "leading by example" matter for ethics?
options: Employees often follow the examples set by their managers
Managers are exempt from ethics rules
Examples replace written policies by law
questions.explain: Leaders shape ethical culture.
questions.evidence: Leading by Example Employees often follow the examples set by their managers.

questions.q: What is the purpose of ethics training programmes?
options: To build awareness of questionable business activities and practise appropriate responses
questions.explain: Many companies have ethics training.
questions.evidence: In addition to providing a system to resolve ethical dilemmas, organizations also provide formal training to develop an awareness of questionable business activities and practice appropriate responses.

questions.q: What is corporate social responsibility (CSR)?
options: A company's duty only to its shareholders
A tax paid by large firms
The concern of businesses for the welfare of society as a whole
questions.explain: Acting ethically is one of four CSR components.
questions.evidence: Acting in an ethical manner is one of the four components of the pyramid of corporate social responsibility (CSR) , which is the concern of businesses for the welfare of society as a whole.

questions.q: Which responsibility forms the foundation of the CSR pyramid?
questions.explain: Legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities build on it.
questions.evidence: Exhibit 2.4 portrays economic responsibility as the foundation for the other three responsibilities.

questions.q: What is philanthropic responsibility in the CSR pyramid?
questions.explain: Economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities together.
questions.evidence: to do what is right, just, and fair (ethical responsibility); and to be a good corporate citizen (philanthropic responsibility).

questions.q: In successful organisations, what does risk management do?
options: Enhances planning and prioritisation, helps achieve objectives and strengthens agility
questions.explain: Risk management is part of planning and decision-making.
questions.evidence: Introduction In successful organisations, risk management enhances strategic planning and prioritisation, assists in achieving objectives and strengthens the ability to be agile to respond to the challenges faced.

questions.q: Where should risk management sit in an organisation, according to the Orange Book?
options: As an essential and integral part of planning and decision-making
questions.explain: It is needed to meet objectives and achieve value for money.
questions.evidence: If we are serious about meeting objectives successfully, improving service delivery and achieving value for money, risk management must be an essential and integral part of planning and decision‑making.

questions.q: How should risk management processes be conducted?
options: Systematically, iteratively and collaboratively, drawing on experts and stakeholders
questions.explain: Principle C3 of the Orange Book.
questions.evidence: C3 - Risk management processes (see Section D) should be conducted systematically, iteratively and collaboratively, drawing on the knowledge and views of experts and stakeholders.

questions.q: What should management information enable, for managing risk?
options: Transparency and timely escalation of risks based on agreed criteria
questions.explain: Informative, transparent information supports good risk management.
questions.evidence: Informative and transparent management information should enable departments and arm’s length bodies to promote transparency and understanding in achieving the effective management of risks, including the timely escalation of risks, as necessary, based on agreed criteria.

questions.q: What do accounting officers sign each year?
options: Statements acknowledging their responsibilities and assuring the adequacy of internal controls
questions.explain: Their control responsibilities safeguard quality and public funds.
questions.evidence: Each year accounting officers sign statements acknowledging their responsibilities and providing assurance on the adequacy of internal controls.

questions.q: Does Part II of the Orange Book add new principles?
options: No: it gives more detail on the 'what' and 'why' of controlling risk
questions.explain: Part II helps the Part I principles be consistently understood.
questions.evidence: Part II: The Risk Control Framework Part II does not introduce any additional principles.

questions.q: In the three lines model, what does the first line do?
options: Owns the risks and runs internal controls day to day
questions.explain: The first line also implements corrective actions.
questions.evidence: The first line ‘own’ the risks and are responsible for execution of the organisation’s response to those risks through executing internal controls on a day-to-day basis and for implementing corrective actions to address deficiencies.

questions.q: What role does the second line play?
options: Supports management with expertise, process excellence and monitoring
questions.explain: It works alongside the first line.
questions.evidence: The second line should support management by bringing expertise, process excellence, and monitoring alongside the first line to help ensure that risks are effectively managed.

questions.q: What does an independent internal audit function provide?
options: An objective evaluation of how effectively the organisation assesses and manages risk
questions.explain: It reviews the first and second lines.
questions.evidence: An independent internal audit function [footnote 15] will, through a risk-based approach to its work, provide an objective evaluation of how effectively the organisation assesses and manages its risks, including the design and operation of the “first and second lines of defence”.

questions.q: Who has some responsibility for risk management?
questions.explain: The three lines model coordinates these roles.
questions.evidence: Annex 2: The Three Lines Model Everyone in an organisation has some responsibility for risk management.

questions.q: What are the three typical steps of money laundering?
questions.explain: In the end, "dirty money" appears "clean".
questions.evidence: Typically, it involves three steps: placement, layering and integration.

questions.q: When was the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) established?
questions.explain: It became a key tool against money laundering.
questions.evidence: The BSA was established in 1970 and has become one of the most important tools in the fight against money laundering.

questions.q: Which crimes can money laundering facilitate?
questions.explain: It can also harm the global economy.
questions.evidence: Money laundering can facilitate crimes such as drug trafficking and terrorism, and can adversely impact the global economy.

questions.q: What is the purpose of customer due diligence?
options: Checking that customers are who they say they are
questions.explain: You must also risk-assess your business.
questions.evidence: These include carrying out ‘customer due diligence’ measures to check that your customers are who they say they are, and risk assessing your business .

questions.q: Who is the beneficial owner?
options: The bank that holds the account
The person behind the customer who owns or controls it, or for whom a transaction is done
The cashier who takes the payment
questions.explain: You must identify the beneficial owner in certain situations.
questions.evidence: The beneficial owner is usually the person who’s behind the customer and who owns or controls the customer, or it’s the person on whose behalf a transaction or activity is carried out.

questions.q: What are linked transactions?
options: Transactions deliberately broken into smaller ones to avoid due diligence checks
Payments made with a linked bank card
questions.explain: Splitting payments below thresholds is a red flag.
questions.evidence: Linked transactions are individual transactions of less than 15,000 euros (or 10,000 euros for high value dealers or art market participants) that have been deliberately broken down into separate, smaller transactions to avoid customer due diligence checks.

questions.q: In a business registered for money laundering supervision, whom must staff report suspicious activity to?
questions.explain: The nominated officer decides whether to report to the NCA.
questions.evidence: If your business is registered for money laundering supervision Anyone in your business must report any suspicious transaction or activity they become aware of to the nominated officer .

questions.q: How does the nominated officer report suspicions to the National Crime Agency?
options: By making a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR)
By cancelling the account without a record
questions.explain: SARs are disclosures to the NCA.
questions.evidence: They do this by making a Suspicious Activity Report ( SAR ).

questions.q: What is the purpose of law, according to the lesson?
options: To keep the system stable while allowing orderly change
questions.explain: The law protects the rights of people and businesses.
questions.evidence: The purpose of law is to keep the system stable while allowing orderly change.

questions.q: What is a contract?
options: An agreement that sets out the relationship between parties regarding a specified action
A promise that cannot be enforced
questions.explain: Valid contracts have required elements.
questions.evidence: A contract is an agreement that sets forth the relationship between parties regarding the performance of a specified action.

questions.q: What are express warranties?
options: Warranties that are neither written nor spoken
Specific statements of fact or promises about a product by the seller
questions.explain: Implied warranties are neither written nor oral.
questions.evidence: Warranties Express warranties are specific statements of fact or promises about a product by the seller.

questions.q: How do implied warranties differ from express warranties?
options: They are always written in the contract
They are spoken by the salesperson
Implied warranties are neither written nor oral
questions.explain: They arise from the law, not from statements.
questions.evidence: Implied warranties are neither written nor oral.

questions.q: What does consumerism reflect?
options: The amount people spend on holidays
The struggle for power between buyers and sellers
questions.explain: Consumer protection laws balance that power.
questions.evidence: Consumer Protection Laws Consumerism reflects the struggle for power between buyers and sellers.

questions.q: What did the Child Protection Act (1966) do?
options: Prohibited the sale of harmful toys
Required all products to be free
questions.explain: It also lets the FDA remove dangerous products.
questions.evidence: Child Protection Act (1966) Prohibits sale of harmful toys and gives the FDA the right to remove dangerous products from the marketplace.

questions.q: How do scammers often target small businesses?
options: By pretending to be government officials or offering "too good to be true" deals
questions.explain: Learn to recognise common scams.
questions.evidence: Scammers often target small businesses by pretending to be government officials or offering “too good to be true” financial deals.

questions.q: What is a warning sign of grant or loan fraud?
options: A request to fill in an official form
A promise of "guaranteed" approval if you pay a fee upfront
A letter with your business name
questions.explain: Real programmes don't guarantee approval for a fee.
questions.evidence: Grant & Loan Fraud: Scammers may contact you promising “guaranteed” approval for an SBA loan or grant if you pay a fee upfront.
